newsitem.title: USA: Oakland USD, Calif., rated single-A by S&P.
newsitem.headline: Oakland USD, Calif., rated single-A by S&P.

text.p: NEW YORK, July 16 - Standard & Poor's today has assigned its single-A' rating to Oakland Unified School District, Calif.'s G.O. capital appreciation bonds (Election of 1994) series 1997B due Aug. 1, 2001-2007, 2021.
Additionally, Standard & Poor's today has affirmed its ratings on the district as follows:
-- Refunding certificates of participation series 1994 at triple-B'-plus, and
-- A large and diverse employment base,
-- Growing student enrollment at a manageable rate,

The rating on the district's certificates also reflects the district's covenant to budget and appropriate lease payments and the strong essentiality of the leased assets -- Oakland High School and two warehouse buildings. The district serves the city of Oakland, which is an integral part of the Bay Area economy. The average daily attendance (ADA) (the count by which the district's state aid is determined) has been increasing, despite a recent teacher's strike in early 1996. 1998's projected 52,418 students marks a 4.3% increase from 1994 ADA of 50,267. While fiscal 1998 will have class sizes of 20 to 1 in grades 1, 2, and 3, class size in other grades are high at 31 to 1 or 32 to 1.

The district continues to manage its finances prudently. Fiscal 1996 closed with an unreserved $8.6 million general fund balance (3.3% of expenditures), slightly higher than previous years due to salary savings from the strike, which lasted over 30 days. The district settled the strike on March 19, 1996 with a contract in place through fiscal 1999. Teacher's wage increases are factored into a balanced 1998 budget. Estimated actuals for fiscal 1997 project an unreserved balance of at least $6.7 million (2.5% of expenditures). The 1998 budget is balanced with an unreserved balance of 2%, the state's minimum requirement for the district. The district receives $7 million in additional revenues to its general fund with the recent passage of a $75 per parcel tax on property owners.

Debt has risen, mainly due to increased borrowing by overlapping entities, however, the district does have $77.5 million of authorized, but unissued debt following this issuance. Overall net debt is high at $3,584 per capita and 8.4% of true value. The district plans to issue the balance of the debt over the next eight years, with a targeted tax rate of $25 per $100,000 of AV, or about $29.50 for the average single family home.

Government, transportation, and utility sectors remain particularly important to Oakland's economic base. The tax base is large and diverse, with the top ten taxpayers comprising only 3.4% of AV and about 50% from single-family residences. AV has climbed steadily at to $16.3 billion in 1997 from 14.7 million in 1993. 1997's increase, however, was only 0.9%. New home sale activity through May 31, 1997, indicate an increase in the average home price for a single-family residence to $227,600 from $208,700 in 1996.
The outlook reflects the district's track record of prudent financial management and manageable capital needs.
